passages.happening:
“This is the account of Esau (that is, Edom)” (verse 1).

Esau's wives and sons are named (verses 2-5). Then Esau takes his whole household, his animals and everything he owns, “and he moved to a land far away from his brother Jacob” (verse 6). “For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together” (verse 7).

“So Esau (that is, Edom) settled in the area of Mount Seir” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Why is there a list of names here? Genesis is built on headings that say ‘This is the account of’. Each one opens a new part of the book. Esau gets his own heading, just as Ishmael did (25:12). The son who was not chosen to carry the promise is not forgotten. God kept his word to him too.

Edom means ‘red’. Genesis links it with Esau's red hair at birth and the red stew he traded his birthright for (25:25, 30). Seir is the rugged hill country south and east of the Dead Sea.

Esau's wives here have different names from the ones in earlier chapters (26:34; 28:9). Readers explain this in several ways: some women were known by more than one name, or separate family records were kept side by side. The text does not explain, and it lets both stand.

Notice verse 7. The land could not hold both brothers' herds. The same was said of Abraham and Lot (13:6). Once again one brother moves away, and once again it happens in peace.
passages.later: God later tells Israel not to take Esau's land: “I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession” (Deuteronomy 2:5). And the law says, “Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).
passages.asks: Genesis makes room for the brother who was not chosen. Ask whom you have quietly left out of your story because they were not on the main road. Then ask how God might still be keeping faith with them.

passages.t: Clans and chiefs, Esau's and Seir's
passages.happening:
“This is the account of Esau, the father of the Edomites, in the area of Mount Seir” (verse 9).

Esau's sons and grandsons are named (verses 10-14). “Timna, a concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz, gave birth to Amalek” (verse 12). Then they are named again as chiefs, the heads of clans (verses 15-19).

Next come the people who lived in Seir before Esau: “the sons of Seir the Horite, who were living in the land” (verse 20), with their families and chiefs (verses 20-30). One of them, Anah, “found the hot springs in the wilderness as he was pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world a list like this did more than record who was whose son. It showed how clans were linked, who led them, and where they lived. It was a kind of map made of names.

Watch a family turn into a people. First Esau's sons are sons. Then they are chiefs. A household is becoming a nation.

Esau's family did not move into an empty land. The Horites were there first. The lists show the two peoples marrying into each other. Esau's wife Oholibamah was a granddaughter of Zibeon, one of the Horite chiefs (verses 2, 20).

One name here will matter later: Amalek. His descendants, the Amalekites, became the first people to attack Israel after it came out of Egypt. Genesis simply names him as Esau's grandson. The Amalekites of the Bible were an ancient people. Nothing here is said against any people living today.

The word in verse 24 that the BSB renders ‘hot springs’ appears only here in the Bible. Its meaning is uncertain. Some older translations read ‘mules’. No teaching hangs on it.
passages.later:
The Amalekites attacked Israel in the wilderness: “the Amalekites came and attacked the Israelites at Rephidim” (Exodus 17:8). Deuteronomy says they fell on the weary stragglers at the back (Deuteronomy 25:17-18).

Some names here return in other books. Job's friend Eliphaz is called a Temanite (Job 2:11), and Job himself lived in the land of Uz (Job 1:1).
passages.asks: A list of names can look like filler, but each name was a person. Ask whose names you skip over in the lives around you. Then ask what it would mean to see them as God does.

passages.t: Kings in Edom before Israel had a king
passages.happening:
“These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites” (verse 31).

Eight kings follow, one after another: Bela, Jobab, Husham, Hadad, Samlah, Shaul, Baal-hanan, and another Hadad (verses 32-39). Then the chiefs of Edom are listed by their places, and the chapter closes: “Esau was the father of the Edomites” (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
Look at the order. Edom has kings while Jacob's family are still herdsmen living in tents in a land they do not own. God had promised Jacob that kings would come from him (35:11). That promise would be slow. Esau's crowns came fast.

Notice too that no king is the son of the king before him. Each comes from a different town. Kingship in Edom seems not to have passed from father to son.

Verse 31 raises a question. ‘Before any king reigned over the Israelites’ sounds like a writer who knew that Israel later had kings. Israel's first king, Saul, came long after Moses. Readers take this in more than one way. Many scholars see the verse as a sign that Genesis reached its final form in the time of Israel's kings or later. Many who hold that Moses was the main author accept that later hands updated such details, much as tradition holds that someone other than Moses wrote the account of his death (Deuteronomy 34). Others say Moses could write this way because kings had already been promised to Jacob's family. The book page on Genesis sets out these views, and these notes do not settle the question.
passages.later:
Edom's later story with Israel was bitter. When Jerusalem fell to Babylon, Edom stood by and joined in. The short book of Obadiah is about that: “Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame and cut off forever” (Obadiah 1:10).

Yet the prophets did not shut Edom out of God's future. Amos saw a day when the house of David would “possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name” (Amos 9:12). James quotes those words in the Greek form when the church welcomes Gentiles: “so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord” (Acts 15:17).
passages.asks: Esau had kings early, and Jacob waited. Ask how you feel when others seem to get quickly what God has promised you slowly. Then ask whether you can trust his timing more than your own.
